sec1.titulo: What a director needs from a briefing
abertura: In your lesson you brief a director about a news article with a lot of numbers in it.
Mark the **three** things a director usually needs from that kind of briefing.

itens.t: Every number in the article, in the order it appears
itens.porque: A director needs the numbers that change a decision. The others can wait until someone asks.

itens.t: What happened, in one or two sentences
itens.porque: Without the story, the numbers have nothing to hang on. One or two sentences is usually enough.

itens.t: Where each important number comes from
itens.porque: A figure from the company and a figure from a consultant are not worth the same, and the director cannot see the article.

itens.t: The article read out word for word
itens.porque: Reading it out takes longer than the director has, and it leaves the choosing to them.

itens.t: Your opinion, before any of the facts
itens.porque: Your reading is useful at the end, marked as yours. Said first, it sounds like one of the facts.

itens.t: Which figures are exact and which are estimates
itens.porque: An estimate repeated as a fact can end up in someone else's presentation as a fact.

sec1.rationale: The story, the source of each important figure, and whether the figure is exact. The rest the director can ask for.

sec3.titulo: Read it once, for the story
abertura: A short news item about a different company. Read it once, without stopping on single words.

doc.texto:
A food-processing company in the interior of São Paulo state says absenteeism at its largest plant rose from 3.1% to 4.7% between January and March, during an unusually hot quarter. The company, which employs about 2,400 people, asked not to be named.

Most of the extra absences were short, one or two days, and most were in the packing area, which has no air conditioning. A union representative said workers had asked for longer breaks “for years.”

An occupational health researcher at a local university estimates that each unplanned absence costs a plant of that size around $180 in overtime and lost output, but she said the number “varies a lot from plant to plant.”

The company says it is installing cooling in two areas and expects to finish before December. It has not said how much the work will cost.

abertura: Mark the **two** sentences that sum up the article.

itens.t: Workers at the plant stopped working because of the heat.
itens.porque: Nobody stopped work. The absences were short, one or two days, and the union talks about breaks.

itens.t: Absences went up at a plant during a hot quarter, and the company is making changes.
itens.porque: The first and the last paragraphs, together: the rise, and the cooling the company is installing.

itens.t: The company has published what the cooling will cost.
itens.porque: The last sentence says the opposite: it has not said how much the work will cost.

itens.t: Most people were absent for more than a week.
itens.porque: The article says most of the extra absences were one or two days.

itens.t: There is an estimate of what an absence costs, and it does not come from the company.
itens.porque: The $180 comes from a researcher at a university, and she says it varies a lot.

sec3.rationale: The story is the rise and the response. The estimate matters because of who it comes from.

abertura: The same news item. Read it again and say where each piece of information comes from.

itens.t: Absenteeism at the largest plant rose from 3.1% to 4.7%.
itens.porque: “A food-processing company … says absenteeism … rose from 3.1% to 4.7%.” The verb says carries the source.

itens.t: One unplanned absence costs around $180.
itens.porque: The occupational health researcher estimates it. The company gives no cost at all.

itens.t: The cooling work will cost about $95,000.
itens.porque: No cost for the cooling appears: “It has not said how much the work will cost.”

itens.t: Workers have wanted longer breaks for a long time.
itens.porque: The union representative: workers asked for longer breaks “for years.”

itens.t: The cooling will be ready before December.
itens.porque: The company says it expects to finish before December. It is the company’s expectation, not something that has happened.

itens.t: The cost of an absence is different in each plant.
itens.porque: The same researcher: the number “varies a lot from plant to plant.”

sec4.rationale: Three sources in four short paragraphs, and one figure that nobody in the article gives.

abertura: Choose the ending that belongs there. All five sentences are about the same news item.

itens.t: Absenteeism rose
itens.porque: From the starting figure to the new one. In English a decimal is said with point: three point one.

itens.t: The company employs
itens.porque: About goes straight before the number, with no of. Two thousand four hundred people.

itens.t: The researcher estimates that an absence
itens.porque: Verb, then around, then the figure. One hundred eighty dollars.

itens.t: The company has not said
alts: how much will the work cost
how much the work will cost
itens.ok: how much the work will cost
itens.porque: Inside a sentence, the question keeps statement order: how much the work will cost.

itens.t: It is installing cooling in two areas and
itens.porque: Expect is followed by to + verb. It marks something that has not happened yet.

abertura: Complete each sentence so that the source, or what is missing, is in the sentence. You can use these sentences in your lesson.
itens: "{According to} the company, absenteeism rose from 3.1% to 4.7%."
"That figure {comes from} a researcher, not from the company."
"The article {does not say} how much the cooling will cost."
"{My reading is} that the heat is only part of the story."

itens.t: Replacing one warehouse worker costs about $4,870.
itens.porque: Brightline Advisory “estimates that replacing one warehouse worker costs about $4,870.” Norvale gives no cost.

itens.t: Overtime hours rose 18.4% between April and June.
itens.porque: “… overtime hours rose 18.4% between April and June, the company says.”

itens.t: The departures cost Norvale $233,800.
itens.porque: Norvale “has not published what the departures cost.” The $233,800 is the consultancy estimate multiplied by 48 people, and the article says they “would represent roughly” that amount.

itens.t: The route will reopen by the end of the year.
itens.porque: “The carriers expect the route to reopen by the end of the year.” It is their expectation.

itens.t: Turnover at the largest site reached 14.6% in the second quarter.
itens.porque: “Company figures show that voluntary turnover at Norvale’s largest site went from 9.2% … to 14.6% in the second.”

itens.t: The detour adds nine to twelve days to each trip.
itens.porque: “The detour adds nine to twelve days to each trip, according to two of the largest carriers.”

ev3.rationale: Two figures from the company, two from the carriers, one estimate from a consultancy, and one statement that sounds like a fact and has no source: the total cost.

itens.t: roughly
itens.porque: “would represent roughly $233,800”. Roughly says the number is rounded and approximate.

itens.t: the company says
itens.porque: “overtime hours rose 18.4% …, the company says.” The source sits at the end of the sentence.

itens.t: has not decided whether
itens.porque: “has not decided whether to hire temporary staff”. Nothing has been decided, so it cannot be reported as a plan.

itens.t: would represent
itens.porque: Would marks a calculation: if the estimate is right, this is the total. Nobody paid this amount on record.

itens.t: expect the route to reopen
itens.porque: “The carriers expect the route to reopen by the end of the year.” An expectation is about the future.

itens.t: according to two of the largest carriers
itens.porque: “The detour adds nine to twelve days …, according to two of the largest carriers.”

cl3.rationale: Two of each. A briefing that drops these words turns an estimate into a fact and an expectation into a plan.

abertura: A quick reference to the situation and the language you used.

tabela: A briefing to a director who has not read a news article full of numbers.
Giving each figure with where it comes from, and saying which ones are estimates.
According to the company,… · Company figures show… · That comes from…, not from…
A consultancy estimates about… · That would be roughly… · That is an estimate, not a company figure.
from 9.2 to 14.6 percent · a rise of 5.4 percentage points · up by more than half
a detour · a carrier · a distribution center · to represent · a shift model

callout.texto: When two percentages are compared, ask: percent of what? The gap between 9.2% and 14.6% is 5.4 percentage points. As a percent of where it started, it is more than half.
